title: Magnetic field induced modulation of heat transport in CrPS$_4$ probed by TaIrTe$_4$ transverse Seebeck thermometry
authors: Krishnaraajan Sundararajan, Sergio Alvarruiz, Cédric A. Cordero-Silis, Majid Ahmadi, Marcos H. D. Guimarães, Jagoda S\lawińska, Joseph Barker, Bart J. van Wees
abstract: Understanding and controlling heat flow in low-dimensional magnetic materials is central to thermoelectrics and spin caloritronics. One of the challenges is the absence of sensitive probes of small, field-dependent modulations in thermal transport. Here we demonstrate transverse Seebeck thermometry using exfoliated TaIrTe$_4$ as a probe of thermal conductivity modulated by an external magnetic field on a van der Waals magnet, CrPS$_4$. With a temperature gradient oriented at $45^\circ$ to its principal crystallographic axes, TaIrTe$_4$ exhibits a transverse thermopower exceeding $200~\mathrm{μV\,K^{-1}}$ for 900 nm wide and 30 $μ$m long electrodes, enabling precise detection of variations in the local temperature gradients. Exploiting this with CrPS$_4$ in a nonlocal geometry, we resolve distinct field dependent thermal conductivity changes associated with both the spin-flip and spin-flop magnetic transitions which we attribute to variations in the magnon$-$phonon coupling in CrPS$_4$. At 5 K, the transverse Seebeck response is modulated by more than 8$\%$ by an external magnetic field, demonstrating strong magnetic control of heat transport in CrPS$_4$. This all van der Waals platform offers high sensitivity to modulations of thermal conductivity and a broad adaptability to a wide range of exfoliated magnetic systems.
summary: This research uses transverse Seebeck thermometry with $	ext{TaIrTe}_4$ to sensitively measure heat transport in the van der Waals magnet $	ext{CrPS}_4$. By applying an external magnetic field, the authors resolve clear modulations in thermal conductivity corresponding to magnetic phase transitions. This demonstrates a powerful, non-invasive platform for studying magnetic control over thermal energy flow.
main_problem: The study aims to understand and control heat flow in low-dimensional magnetic materials by investigating the magnetic field-induced modulation of thermal conductivity.
main_result: The researchers successfully detected distinct, field-dependent changes in the thermal conductivity of $	ext{CrPS}_4$ associated with its spin-flip and spin-flop magnetic transitions, attributing this to variations in magnon–phonon coupling.
method: Transverse Seebeck thermometry is employed using exfoliated $	ext{TaIrTe}_4$ as a highly sensitive, non-invasive thermal probe on the van der Waals magnet $	ext{CrPS}_4$.
model_or_system: The system involves a layered van der Waals antiferromagnet ($	ext{CrPS}_4$) whose thermal transport properties are modulated by an external magnetic field, measured using a two-dimensional semi-metal ($	ext{TaIrTe}_4$) as the sensing element.
key_observables: Transverse thermopower (exceeding $200 \mu	ext{V K}^{-1}$), field-dependent modulation of thermal conductivity ($\kappa$), and the thermoelectric voltage response ($\Delta V/V$).
important_parameters: Low temperature (e.g., 5 K), magnetic field strength (near spin-flop/spin-flip transitions), and temperature gradient orientation relative to crystal axes.
main_assumptions: The transverse Seebeck effect provides a non-invasive, nonlocal probe for magnetic heat transport, and the observed modulation is primarily due to changes in magnon–phonon coupling.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the crystal structure and device geometry of $	ext{TaIrTe}_4$, showing how the transverse voltage response is measured when the temperature gradient is oriented at $45^\circ$ to the principal axes.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the need for sensitive thermal probes in magnetic materials, details the use of $	ext{TaIrTe}_4$ for transverse Seebeck thermometry, and presents measurements demonstrating the magnetic field's ability to modulate $	ext{CrPS}_4$'s thermal conductivity across magnetic transitions.
why_interesting: This work provides an experimental demonstration of using thermoelectric effects to probe subtle, magnetically induced changes in thermal transport, which is a key area bridging condensed matter physics and thermal energy management.
